articles.title: These Are The Weapons Ukraine Used To Drop The Kerch Bridge
articles.text:
Ukraine has revealed a remarkably diverse collection of domestically developed weapons, and at least two foreign-supplied ones, used in its latest attack on the Kerch Bridge, the critical road and rail link connecting occupied Crimea with mainland Russia. You can read what we know about the operation in our separate coverage here.

The operation, coordinated by Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) and the General Staff, unfolded over several weeks and involved seven stages, according to President Volodymyr Zelensky. The Ukrainian leader made the disclosures today, in a post on his official X account, accompanied by a video of the latest strike. As well as the bridge itself, Ukrainian forces systematically targeted Russian air defense systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other installations before moving against the main target.

The final assault, conducted overnight on November 16-17, involved a combination of long-range attack drones, cruise missiles, and shorter-range drones, according to Zelensky. He explained that Palianytsia drones struck the bridge’s road section, while FP-5 Flamingo, Neptune, and Ruta cruise missiles were used against the railway section.

In a retro-styled meme video posted on X today, the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense presented imagery of the bridge before and after the attacks, overlaid with pictures of some of the weapons used in the operation. For the FP-5 missile, however, its photo was replaced with a flock of flamingos. The result mimics the opening credits for the TV series Santa Barbara, which was popular in the immediate post-Soviet era.

The Ukrainian president named 11 weapons systems involved in the broader operation. Here is a closer look at what we know about them.

Dovbush

Type: Uncrewed aerial vehicle

Dovbush is a family of Ukrainian-developed uncrewed aircraft, with variants intended for reconnaissance and strike missions. Public information on the specific variant employed in the Kerch Bridge operation remains limited.

The Dovbush family includes longer-range platforms, with some versions reportedly designed to operate deep inside enemy territory. Ukrainian forces have used Dovbush aircraft in the broader campaign against Russian military infrastructure. The family also includes heavy ‘drone motherships,’ used to deliver smaller attack drones closer to their targets before launching them.

Since the specific variant or targets assigned to the system during the operation are unclear, the drone may have been used for reconnaissance or strike missions, or both.

Vendetta

Type: FPV attack drone

Vendetta is a Ukrainian attack drone associated with the country’s expanding family of domestically produced uncrewed systems. It is described in Ukrainian reporting as an FPV loitering munition, with thermal-imaging capability supporting operations at night. Previous Ukrainian reports describe it as a ‘relatively inexpensive middle-strike drone,’ in a class of drones with a range of between 12 and 43 miles.

There is little publicly available information about its precise role in the campaign. However, an attack drone with a ‘main-in-the-loop’ capability such as this could well have been used in the effort to systematically dismantle Russian electronic warfare and air defense capabilities before and during the main attack, including responding to dynamic or ‘pop-up’ threats. Bearing in mind the typical range of such drones, there is a question as to whether Vendetta was launched in the vicinity of the target, or if it was delivered via another drone, which would have required its feed to be relayed to operators via satcom. Launch of the drone from a sea-based platform of some kind, operating off the Crimean coast, would be another option.

Da Vinci

Type: Long-range one-way attack drone

Da Vinci is another uncrewed system identified by Zelensky. The propeller-driven drone is manufactured by Netherlands-based defense technology company Destinus and is reportedly intended to operate in contested electronic warfare environments.

Da Vinci is understood to be closely related to the Lord drone from Destinus, which can reportedly travel more than 621 miles, carry a warhead weighing between 88 and 220 pounds, and be prepared for launch in just 15 minutes.

Although the precise configuration employed in this operation has not been disclosed, unconfirmed reports state Da Vinci was used to suppress Russian air defenses.

Sichen

Type: Long-range one-way attack drone

Sichen is a Ukrainian long-range strike drone designed to attack targets deep behind enemy lines. Based on its appearance, it clearly owes much to the Iranian-designed Shahed-136, also widely employed by Russia.

Publicly reported specifications put its range at up to approximately 870 miles, with a warhead weighing as much as 88 pounds.

Its inclusion in the Kerch Bridge operation points to the breadth of Ukraine’s long-range drone arsenal. However, Zelensky did not specify which installations Sichen targeted.

MICH-2000

Type: Long-range attack drone

Another Shahed-lookalike, MICH-2000 is a Ukrainian long-range one-way attack drone associated with the SBU’s Alpha special operations unit.

The aircraft is reportedly based on a modified commercial Chinese UAV design and adapted for military strike missions. Ukraine’s use of readily available commercial designs as the basis for its own strike drones is by now well established, although more recently it has relied more heavily on fully domestic products.

Some reporting puts its operational range at approximately 1,240 miles, although publicly available performance information remains limited.

Its participation in the operation is noteworthy because it demonstrates the variety of platforms Ukraine is employing for deep-strike missions, including systems developed outside its traditional aerospace industry.

Ruta

Type: Cruise missile

Ruta is a Ukrainian-operated, European-developed, low-cost cruise missile ‘strike system’ manufactured by Destinus.

According to the manufacturer, the baseline Ruta Block 1 is designed to deliver precision strikes against high-value military targets at ranges of up to 186 miles. It carries a payload of up to 331 pounds.

Destinus describes the system as being optimized for high-volume salvo attacks, with an emphasis on cost efficiency. It is designed to fly at low altitude, using terrain masking to help penetrate enemy air defenses.

One of its key features is a multi-sensor navigation system combining inertial navigation, satellite navigation, and visual navigation. Destinus says this architecture is intended to allow the weapon to continue operating in environments where electronic warfare systems are attempting to disrupt satellite navigation.

The company describes Ruta Block 1 as its baseline configuration, with two additional versions also identified: Block 2, offering extended range, and Block 3, designed for long-range deep-strike missions.

Ruta reportedly began arriving in Ukraine in 2024. The first firmer evidence of their operational use appeared earlier this year.

Zelensky specifically identified Ruta among the weapons used against the railway section of the Kerch Bridge, but not the particular version employed. In a post on LinkedIn, Destinus said that Ruta missiles struck the Kerch Bridge on two consecutive days. “Last night’s strikes damaged the bridge’s upper load-bearing structure. Today, seven Ruta missiles hit the bridge, causing one span to collapse,” it added.

Palianytsia

Type: Long-range drone

Palianytsia is one of Ukraine’s more distinctive domestically developed weapons. It is a turbojet-powered drone designed to attack targets at long distances.

Ukraine first publicly acknowledged its successful use in August 2024. The system was developed as part of the country’s effort to expand its ability to conduct deep strikes without relying exclusively on foreign-supplied missiles, which typically come with a restrictive set of employment rules.

Zelensky credited Palianytsia with striking the bridge’s road section during the final phase of the operation.

Its use against such a heavily defended and strategically important target represents a significant demonstration of Ukraine’s growing domestic strike capabilities.

An-197

Type: Uncrewed aerial system

An-197 is among the lesser-known weapons included in Zelensky’s list.

Ukrainian reporting has linked the designation with a long-range strike drone derived from the country’s existing family of deep-strike unmanned aircraft.

Publicly available technical information remains particularly sparse, and its precise relationship to other Ukrainian drone designs is not fully established.

Zelensky did not disclose which targets it was assigned during the operation.

FP-1

Type: Long-range one-way attack drone

FP-1 is a well-known long-range Ukrainian attack drone developed by Fire Point, the company also responsible for the FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile. You can read our previous wide-ranging interview with the company CEO, Iryna Terekh, here.

The system is designed to strike targets deep inside enemy territory and has become part of Ukraine’s expanding domestic deep-strike arsenal.

Its inclusion in the operation underscores how Ukraine employed a combination of different uncrewed platforms, with different levels of performance and payload capabilities, to attack Russian military installations before the final assault on the bridge.

FP-5 Flamingo

Type: Ground-launched cruise missile

The FP-5 Flamingo is one of Ukraine’s most ambitious domestically developed long-range weapons.

Manufactured by Fire Point, the ground-launched cruise missile is designed to attack fixed targets at considerable distances. The manufacturer has advertised a maximum range of approximately 1,864 miles and a warhead weighing up to 2,646 pounds.

The Flamingo is a considerably larger weapon than most of Ukraine’s one-way attack drones and is intended to deliver a substantial explosive payload against high-value targets. When the weapon was first unveiled, TWZ noted that its combination of range and heavy warhead — as well as the absence of foreign restrictions on its use — made it a particularly suitable candidate for going after tougher targets far beyond the frontlines.

Zelensky specifically highlighted the system’s role in the Kerch Bridge operation, saying Ukrainian forces used it to conduct a precision-guided strike. He also noted that the communications link remained operational until the final seconds; this is supported by a purported video from one of the missiles during its final run-in to the target.

The weapon’s reported involvement is especially noteworthy given the bridge’s extensive defensive arrangements, although it also needs to be considered that the Flamingo only made its way through to the target thanks to a wide-ranging effort by a wide variety of other systems.

R-360 Neptune

Type: Anti-ship and land-attack cruise missile

The R-360 Neptune is Ukraine’s domestically developed cruise missile, originally designed to attack naval vessels. It is essentially a Ukrainian version of the Soviet-era Kh-35 anti-ship missile, which has been fielded in air-launched, ground-launched, and ship-launched versions.

Neptune gained international attention in April 2022 when Ukrainian forces used the missiles to strike and sink the Russian Black Sea Fleet flagship Moskva.

The missile has since been adapted for land-attack missions, broadening its role beyond its original anti-ship purpose.

The baseline R-360 has a publicly reported range of approximately 186 miles and a warhead weighing around 331 pounds. Longer-range developments of the Neptune family have also been reported.

Zelensky identified Neptune missiles as among the weapons used against the railway section of the Kerch Bridge, although the specific version involved was not stated.

Its participation highlights how Ukraine has expanded the utility of existing missile designs to address a much wider range of battlefield requirements.

A Multi-Layered Ukrainian Strike

The Kerch Bridge operation illustrates the increasingly diverse nature of Ukraine’s domestic weapons industry — as well as the challenges of prosecuting well-defended targets at extended ranges.

To get around this conundrum, Ukrainian forces appear to have combined reconnaissance and strike platforms, long-range one-way attack drones, jet-powered missile-drones, and conventional cruise missiles. Each of these is suited to a particular target set.

As expected, the operation involved a deliberate effort to degrade the defensive systems protecting the bridge before the final attack. Exactly how this was coordinated once the attack was underway is unclear. Undoubtedly, it was a complex operation that would have required months (at least) or careful planning.

As well as putting Russian air defenses under pressure in terms of the sheer volume of targets in the sky, these Ukrainian systems have a widely varying spectrum of performance and flight profiles, making the process of hunting them down and destroying them that much harder. That being said, we don’t know exactly how many Ukrainian drones and missiles were launched, and what percentage of those made it through to their targets. In any event, a significant degree of attrition by Russian air defenses, not to mention other issues, is a given.

Importantly, Zelensky’s announcement does not provide a weapon-by-weapon account of the first six stages, which will have almost certainly involved many more different systems, nor does it identify the specific targets that every named system engaged.

Nevertheless, the announcement provides an unusually detailed look at the range of Ukrainian weapons involved in an operation against one of Russia’s most heavily defended and symbolically important infrastructure targets.

articles.title: America's hyperscale bit barns draw as much power as entire states
articles.text:
Just 403 hyperscale datacenters consumed an estimated 1.8 percent of US electricity in 2024-25, and their carbon dioxide emissions were roughly two to three times an earlier forecast for 2018.

Research led by the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the Harvard Data Science Initiative looked specifically at hyperscale facilities, the largest class of server farms that typically support cloud computing and AI processing.

The published study, "Assessing the carbon emissions and energy consumption of US hyperscale data centres," estimates their combined electricity use approached that of a single state such as Indiana, Michigan, or Tennessee under the highest-load scenario.

The researchers identified 403 hyperscale facilities by using a larger datacenter dataset, satellite imagery, and building footprints on OpenStreetMap.

Rather than reading electricity meters, the researchers worked out consumption from each site's electrical capacity, the hours in a year, and assumptions about how heavily the facility was running.

Across four operating scenarios, ranging from low-intensity use to AI-heavy workloads, electricity draw was believed to total 68-99 terawatt-hours (TWh). Each of those states consumed approximately 100 TWh during the study period.

The researchers also calculated carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions using eGRID2023 plant-level generation and emissions data from the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). Emissions ranged from 21 million to 31 million metric tons of CO2 across the scenarios, with a central estimate of 25.7 million. That compares with 10.5 million for 2018.

The study covered May 2024 to April 2025, so electricity demand and carbon emissions are likely to be even higher now, the researchers say.

"What we're seeing is already striking, but it's only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry," said Gianluca Guidi, lead author on the paper and postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at Harvard.

"The datacenter boom hasn't slowed down since our study period ended in April 2025. New facilities have been built, existing campuses have expanded, and demand for AI computing continues to grow. That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we're reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026."

Harvard's report also considers the mix of fuels being used to generate the electricity that powers all those hyperscale data houses. The mix varies considerably between regional grids, so where a hyperscale facility is built makes a substantial difference to its attributed emissions.

Across the sites studied, roughly 54 percent of the electricity attributed to their consumption came from fossil fuels, mainly natural gas and coal. The electricity attributed to these facilities nevertheless had a lower average carbon intensity than the US grid overall.

The researchers acknowledge limitations, including that there wasn't enough available data to study all hyperscale sites in the US, and that the data did not allow them to differentiate between power used for general-purpose compute versus AI-specialized operations at individual campuses. ®

OpenAI had publicly reported only 27 such incidents, showing that "OpenAI’s public reports do not represent the full scope of loss-of-control incidents involving OpenAI’s models that have impacted third parties," the lawsuit said. OpenAI "knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it," Bonta said in a press release.

articles.title: Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer
articles.text:
The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration.

Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. The water can be released through turbines, generating electricity on demand. But an extreme, prolonged drought in the Colorado River Basin has resulted in dangerously low water levels in the Southwest’s two largest reservoirs, affecting the availability of this power source.

Residents and farmers in the US Southwest, a region that includes Arizona, New Mexico, and parts of Nevada and California, rely on water that melts in the spring from snowpack in the mountains and is slowly allowed to flow south via dam releases. Snowfall in the Rocky Mountains provides about 85% of the annual flow of the Colorado River. And in recent years, the river has seen record-low flows. 

Two reservoirs along the Colorado River, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, have struggled to stay above the minimum level required for hydropower plants. At the end of September, Lake Powell’s depth was 3,518 feet, less than 1% above the level required to run the water through turbines that produce electricity at the Glen Canyon power plant. The Hoover Dam power plant requires 950 feet in Lake Mead, and that reservoir was 9% above the minimum in September.

Together, the two plants produced nearly seven terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, enough to serve over 2 million people. 

Low water levels have been an ongoing struggle for the region, which has been in a drought for 27 years. Meanwhile, climate change is continuing to shift rainfall and snowfall patterns across the region and around the world. 

The effects of climate change on hydropower aren’t entirely straightforward globally—some regions will see more rain and snow because of shifting weather patterns, while others are likely to see less. 

But it’s playing a role for hydropower availability, according to one 2022 review study. Rising temperatures bring more droughts, warmer winters means less snow and ice to fill the reservoirs, and more variability in precipitation can lead to alternating floods and droughts, making the power source less reliable. 

Hydropower production is likely to be at its lowest level in over a decade in 2026 and tick even lower in 2027, according to projections from the EIA.

El Niño could provide some temporary relief. Sometimes this weather pattern can mean cooler, wetter conditions for the southern US. Heavy rains brought floods to the region in October and early November, and the water levels in Lake Powell rose more than 20 feet from their mid-September low. But the water is still quite low, and it’ll take much more to help reservoirs recover from decades of drought conditions.

Even as a changing climate complicates the availability of hydropower, the decline in capacity could push greenhouse-gas emissions higher. In 2023, energy-related greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 1.1% globally. A worldwide shortfall in hydropower generation accounted for about 40% of that rise, according to a report from the International Energy Agency.

articles.text: A federal judge on Tuesday blocked President Donald Trump's administration from restricting the types of internships and other practical training opportunities available to international students attending US universities on visas.US District Judge Julia Kobick in Boston issued an injunction barring the US Department of Homeland Security from enforcing two August directives that higher education groups said had abruptly disrupted training opportunities for foreign students nationwide.Kobick, an appointee of former Democratic President Joe Biden, ruled in a lawsuit filed last month by four organizations, including the Association of American Universities and the Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration.It marked the latest victory for plaintiffs challenging efforts by the Trump administration to impose restrictions on student visa holders as part of its hardline immigration agenda. On Monday, a different federal judge in Boston struck down a new rule that would limit how long ‌foreign students can remain in the US without applying for extensions.DHS declined to comment.The education groups in the case before Kobick argued that DHS had sharply narrowed rules that for more than 35 years governed international students' participation in internships and other practical training through a program known as curricular practical training, or CPT.They said foreign students historically could take part in school-authorized internships and training opportunities as long as they were directly related to their field of study and formed an integral part of an established curriculum.According to the plaintiffs, the government long interpreted that standard to allow participation when training either carried academic credit or was required to earn a degree.Amazon and Tesla were the top two employers of CPT students in 2024, when 140,775 student visa holders were authorized to participate in CPT overall, according to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement.But in August, DHS, which oversees ICE, issued messages telling universities that internships and other opportunities qualified only if they were mandatory for every student in a degree program and did not cover elective training taken for academic credit.The agency said it had seen an increase in CPT authorizations it believed did not comply with program requirements and would increase scrutiny of approvals.Kobick found the directives were likely arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act as DHS had failed to acknowledge that it was making a "fundamental" change to the government's longstanding interpretation of the program's rules."Correct or not, this new interpretation is inconsistent with the government's previous position," she wrote.

articles.title: Inspiring FOSS project Crosspoint Reader has lessons about tech, communities, and LLMs
articles.text:
The Ubuntu Summit isn't all about Ubuntu, or even Linux. The second day opened with a talk from CrossPoint Reader project lead Justin Mitchell, with both good and bad news for all kinds of FOSS.

The talk, EPUBs, ESP32s, and Everyone's A Developer Now, was all about a FOSS project that isn't Linux-based – because the devices it targets are much too small to run even the smallest, most cut-down distro.

Recently, a new generation of roughly credit-card sized ebook readers has been thriving. Some have integral magnets, which let them cling to the back of iPhones – or to models with magnetically attached wireless chargers, anyway. The idea is that instead of waking your phone and doom-scrolling, you flip it over and read a book. They are bringing about what Mitchell calls "the Tiktok-ification of reading."

Many of them, though, come from their various manufacturers significantly limited by their original OSes. The strong sales are linked to the availability of free, open-source, cross-platform alternative firmware, which removes many of the restrictions that the devices ship with. For most of them, that means Crosspoint Reader. Some devices are now shipping, new, with versions of Crosspoint Reader.

This runs on multiple different models of compact e-readers, and this small community project has seen impressively widespread adoption: over 300,000 installations. Early in his talk, project lead Mitchell mentioned more than 1,600 forks on GitHub, but at the time of writing, that's up to 2,300 and counting. He estimates nearly half a million users. This kind of success forced Crosspoint Reader to change from being FOSS code to a product. A peripheral example is the Brick Club List, a list of what versions work with what devices – an Excel spreadsheet that grew into a website.

If you haven't been paying attention, you may not have noticed just how much e-readers have shrunk – in size and in cost – in the last few years. The Reg FOSS desk first noticed this trend in 2024, when we read about the smartphone-sized Onyx Palma, which sold for around $300 (about £225). As it happens, this was a decade after The Register first looked at one of Boox's devices. Mini e-readers – and their prices – have continued shrinking since. The $99 (£75) Xteink X4 Classic has a 4.- inch (10.9 cm) screen, and the $79 (£59) Xteink X3 is even smaller: it's the size of a credit card, with a 3.7-inch (9.4 cm) screen. As a result of their strong sales, there are now multiple similar devices on sale, such as the Boox Picco.

The project's GitHub page lists 11 devices it currently supports, all of which are based around the ESP32-C3 system on a chip. The ESP32-C series chips are more powerful than the earlier models of ESP32 microcontrollers: they have a single RISC-V core, but running in the low hundreds of MHz and with some 400 kB of RAM, of which about 380 kB is available. It's very little space, but enough to have fun.

Mitchell talked about some of the problems of being a FOSS project that is used by nearly half a million non-techie people. For many of Crosspoint Reader's users, it's the first time they have ever used open source. Some want tech support. Many demand features that can't fit into these tiny devices. Even when the requests are modest and feasible, such a large user base means that people want a wide range of functionality – and thanks to inexpensive cloud LLMs, even totally non-technical users can try to add new functions for themselves. The result is multiple code submissions every day. Many might fit on their own, but it's impossible to fit them all in. So many queries and submissions puts considerable stress on the volunteer maintainers.

Mitchell mentioned a possibility that they – and we – had never dreamed of: that of pull requests (GitHub parlance for code submissions) from people using such extensive automation that the submitters don’t realize that they’re sending them. One submitter sent 10,000 pull requests in a single month. The problems aren't just technical, or workload-related: there's also a delicate balance of how to refuse well-intentioned and technologically viable submissions that just won't fit for non-technical reasons, such as being too niche for the typical use-case of a sub-£60 gadget.

The problem is that this FOSS firmware is making these cheap gadgets so much more useful that re-flashing them is an implicit part of the purchase. That introduces all kinds of unexpected side-effects, for the users and for the developers. Crosspoint Reader is a microcosm of the rapid growth of Linux and FOSS in general – and a taste of what will happen if it ever goes truly mainstream with mass-market consumers. One of his "what I got wrong about this job" points we particularly liked was:

“The scarce resource isn’t code. We have more code than we know what to do with."

Instead, it's… "Judgement. Trust. Responsibility."

There are lessons for the whole IT industry in there, we reckon. Even for the biggest players.

In the meantime, though, these tiny cheap e-readers are an interesting new thing. As Mitchell put it, paraphrasing The Atlantic, they're:

"Fun in a way gadgets haven’t been for a long time."

Just being fun is a goal that is far too often forgotten… Especially in FOSS. ®

SAP chief customer officer Thomas Saueressig is leaving the German software giant to become CEO of hosting and cloud provider Ionos.

The ERP and biz application vendor confirmed his departure on Tuesday, saying he will remain responsible for his current duties until the end of March 2027. He will succeed Ionos CEO Achim Weiß on April 1.

In January, Saueressig will begin handing over responsibilities to Emmanuel Raptopoulos, currently a regional customer success president, who will take charge on an interim basis. SAP's supervisory board is searching for a permanent successor.

Saueressig joined SAP's executive board in 2019 and became chief customer officer in April 2026. He leads the Customer Value Group and is charged with overseeing sales, customer success, services, and delivery, including adoption of SAP's cloud and AI products.

In previous roles at SAP, Saueressig was responsible for customer services and delivery. He has also led product engineering, and has served as SAP's in-house CIO responsible for IT strategy and cloud transformation. He joined SAP in 2004 through its combined work-and-study program.

His departure follows several changes at the top of SAP in recent years. In September 2024, CTO Jürgen Müller left by mutual agreement following an "incident" at a company event earlier in the year.

In a statement, Müller said his behavior had been inappropriate. The company announced he would get paid €7.1 million following his departure.

Chief revenue officer Scott Russell also left in 2024 by mutual agreement with the supervisory board. Julia White left the role of chief marketing and solutions officer in August 2024.

"Thomas Saueressig has been a valued member of the Executive Board and has made significant contributions to SAP's transformation," said Pekka Ala-Pietilä, chair of SAP's supervisory board. "Over many years, he has helped sharpen SAP's focus on execution, customer value and operational excellence. We thank him for his commitment and wish him all the best for the future."

Saueressig's departure comes as SAP pushes to move the ERP systems underpinning thousands of customers' businesses into the cloud – an effort whose operations and infrastructure he helped oversee. ®

articles.title: Opting out of Gemini tracking? Google will still hold your data 20x longer
articles.text:
Opting out of Gemini chat retention is about to mean a lot less thanks to a quietly announced Google update.

Google on Monday said that it was making changes to Gemini chat history that, at first glance, makes it seem like users are simply getting more control over their discussions with the Chocolate Factory’s chatbot.

At the core of the announcement is Google's splitting of Gemini chat history settings from AI model training permissions. What that means is that users will now be able to store their chat histories with Gemini without also having to opt in to allow their conversations to be used to train those same models, as was previously the case.

So far so good: Being able to have Gemini remember more of your past interactions to contextualize newer discussions is nice, to be sure. The second part of the announcement, however, might raise one's privacy hackles.

"Now, if you turn your new History setting off, future chats will be saved for around two months," Google notes. "They're used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public."

Google said it is making that change in the name of making Gemini safer and more secure, but it fails to mention that the chat retention period for users who turned their history off had been just 72 hours before this update.

That's right: Prior to Monday's change, Gemini users who turned off the "Keep Activity" option only had their chats retained for three days, according to an archived copy of the same page that now states that choosing the same please-don't-store-my-AI-chats option means Google keeps them "for around two months."

It's also worth noting that, even if users have the option to not store Gemini chat records enabled, submitting a feedback request on any Gemini post means that temporary retention period gets extended to three years. That was the case both before and after Monday's change, mind you, but for the privacy-conscious it's definitely important to note.

Sending feedback to Google about a Gemini response also means that humans will be reviewing that particular conversation, as well as any associated files and conversations that can be associated with the one in question. Submitting feedback also means that Google assumes the right to use the conversation and its associated content to improve its services and improve its AI models.

In other words, even if you opt out of having your conversations stored, your Gemini history could still end up being used to feed the Google machine. The company didn't respond to questions for this story. ®

articles.text:
It can be hard to use Google products—or even the Internet itself—without coming into contact with Gemini AI. That is, of course, by design. The more you use Gemini, the more data Google collects to train and improve its generative AI chatbot. The options to limit training on your data have been scant, but Google is finally adding more controls to the Gemini app.

The change currently rolling out to Gemini will separate your chat history from training, which allows you to retain basic AI functionality without handing Google quite so much control over your data. Prior to this change, the only way to opt out of contributing your chat contents (including attachments) for training was to turn off your history. That made it impossible to go back and pick up a chat down the road.

As the new settings roll out, users will see separate toggles for model training and chat history. The history setting will continue to support an adjustable limit, but you will no longer have to change it to stop Google from training on your Gemini usage. Meanwhile, AI training will be an opt-out situation. You'll need to find the toggle to block Google from using your chats for AI training. It's under Activity in the Gemini settings. articles.text:
Two terrorists of the Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT), who were behind the Kulgam attack, have been killed in an encounter with security forces in Jammu and Kashmir.
Key area commander Latief Ahmad Bhat was among the two terrorists who were killed by the security forces in a joint operation.
The gunfight broke out during a cordon and search operation that was launched to track the terrorists behind the November 11 Kulgam attack in which three CRPF personnel were injured.
The killing of Bhat is a major blow to the Lashkar-e-Taiba, as he was the last active local commander in the Kashmir Valley. He was carrying a bounty of Rs 15 lakh.
Acting on actionable Intelligence, the Jammu and Kashmir Police, along with the Rashtriya Rifles, launched a cordon and search operation to gun down the terrorists.
An intense gun battle broke out after the terrorists opened fire on the security forces.
Latief Bhat, also known as Mohammad Lateef Bhat, was a top commander of the Lashkar-e-Taiba. He is linked to several attacks in the Valley, including the killing of migrant workers at Kulgam in July this year.
Bhat (22) hailed from the Khrewan Chader village in Kulgam. He reportedly left home in November 2025 before joining the Lashkar-e-Taiba.
He was also behind the killing of two special police officers — Babi Chand and Yashpal Kumar in Kishtwar district. The two SPOs were on their way back to join the Army.
Following the incidents, Jammu and Kashmir was placed under very high alert.
The security forces are carrying out sanitisation operations at the encounter site. The search operations are ongoing to hunt down the remaining accomplices, including a foreign terrorist. The entire area has been cordoned off by the police and Army personnel.
The killing of Bhat has been a major success for the security agencies.
Bhat had become a headache for the agencies as he had learnt the art of carrying out small-scale attacks and then escape.
He would merge into the local population after an attack, which had made tracking him very difficult. He was directed by his handlers based in Pakistan. The ISI sought to further its local network in Kashmir with the help of Bhat.

articles.title: Hackers smash 'n' grab AI vendor: Take  off with license data of Uber drivers
articles.text:
Uber has confirmed that nearly 150,000 people had their personal information compromised after hackers broke into one of its AI suppliers.

A filing with Oregon's attorney general puts the number of victims at 149,346. Among the data the crooks got their hands on were images of drivers' licenses and information extracted from them, including names, home addresses, dates of birth, and license numbers.

Uber doesn't name the supplier in its filings with US state attorneys general, but told TechCrunch it was Fireworks AI, the inference outfit whose security woes we covered last week.

According to a breach notification filed with Iowa's attorney general, Fireworks alerted Uber to the intrusion on October 9. Uber cut off the supplier's access to its data and, four days later, established that the attackers had accessed drivers' personal information on October 7.

Uber had set up a dedicated cloud storage environment for the AI biz, complete with security monitoring overseen by its own cloud security team. Unfortunately for Uber and its drivers, the crooks were using legitimate credentials, so none of the alarms went off.

The ride-hailing firm says those credentials couldn't be used to access its other systems, and says it has since revoked or changed the credentials associated with the supplier.

Uber hasn't said why it handed images of thousands of driver's licenses to an AI inference outfit. The Register has put that question to both companies, and asked Uber if any drivers outside the US had their data exposed.

Fireworks, which provides infrastructure for developers to run and fine-tune AI models, had a particularly miserable October. The company first disclosed a security incident on October 9 after discovering that someone had been using its internal credentials without permission.

Fireworks initially said it had no evidence that the intruders had gotten their hands on personal information or customer datasets. The company was hacked again later that month and, on November 9, disclosed that some customer data had indeed been compromised.

The AI biz acknowledged that attackers had accessed billing records, some customer datasets, and incomplete model weights. Productivity software maker Notion was among those affected, with some of its customers' conversations with its AI assistant exposed.

Fireworks suspects the involvement of financially motivated criminals in the business of flogging unauthorized access to large language models. Whether the crooks have any plans for the haul of Uber drivers' personal information is unclear.

Uber began notifying affected individuals on November 10, more than a month after learning of the breach. It's offering victims free credit monitoring and fraud assistance, though drivers have just 90 days from the date of their letter to sign up.

This isn't Uber's first brush with cybercriminals in recent months. In August, the ride-hailing giant's logistics arm, Uber Freight, confirmed a break-in after the Helix extortion crew claimed to have made off with almost a million files, including data pilfered from mailboxes and OneDrive accounts. ®

Britain’s Prince William and Kate Middleton took part in a game of street cricket in Mumbai on Monday, the first day of a three-day trip that marks the Princess of Wales’ most high-profile overseas visit since undergoing treatment for cancer in 2024.

They will then meet the finalists for the Earthshot Prize awards, which will be announced on Tuesday.
Founded in 2020 by heir-to-the-throne William, the Earthshot Prize aims to find solutions to climate change, and awards five winners £1 million ($1.3 million) each to scale up their projects.
The couple will conclude their visit with a meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi.
Kate, 44, underwent preventative chemotherapy for an unspecified form of cancer, after which she significantly reduced her official workload. Now in remission, she has gradually increased her public appearances, but had not joined William on previous foreign trips.
Her only significant overseas visit since 2024 was in May, when she travelled alone to Italy for two days as part of her work focusing on early childhood development.

articles.title: Windows 11 previews remote padlock only IT can open
articles.text:
A new experimental Windows 11 build previews security features including an Intune-controlled Remote Lock, while a beta build clears away another relic from the halcyon days of Windows Phone.

The security changes include viewing and individually removing passkeys stored on FIDO2 (Fast Identity Online 2) security keys, plus a preview of the Microsoft Pluton Cryptographic Provider. For enterprise administrators, though, Remote Lock is the main attraction.

Finding a lost Windows device has been around for years, and you can also remotely wipe a device to prevent data from falling into the wrong hands. Remote Lock lets an administrator lock a managed device through Intune without wiping it. The instruction takes effect at the device's next check-in. Windows signs out of every active session, hides every sign-in option, and shows a locked screen.

The lock survives restarts and the device going offline – only an administrator can lift it remotely. Microsoft's documentation spells out the restriction: "There is no offline or local unlock. No PIN, password, local admin, or web sign-in works on a locked device; unlock arrives only through Intune."

Once the lock is applied, even stolen credentials won't restore access through the normal sign-in screen. The user's account itself is not affected; this applies only to the specific device.

Though still in preview, the feature will allow IT teams to respond non-destructively to a report of a missing device. It doesn't erase data or isolate the device from the network (Microsoft directs admins to other Intune controls if that is required).

The lock doesn't block Safe Mode, Windows Recovery Environment, or booting from external media. Microsoft advises keeping BitLocker enabled to protect the data.

Now for the beta build, where Microsoft, in time-honored fashion, gives and takes away. The latest Windows Insider build hammers another nail into the coffin of Microsoft Maps.

The Maps app was removed from the Microsoft Store and made nonfunctional in July 2025. Now Offline Maps settings are following it out, as Microsoft retires the Windows UWP Map control and Windows Maps platform APIs.

The original Maps app dates back to Windows Phone 7 and appeared on the desktop with Windows 8. It continued through subsequent versions before Microsoft stopped preinstalling it with Windows 11 version 24H2.

For those with a nostalgic streak, it's another piece of Windows Phone disappearing off the map. ®

articles.text:
Aerospace propulsion company Vayuvya Defence have successfully tested their Vayu 250 micro jet engine, which is part of their work developing homegrown small jet propulsion technology. They announced the news on 15th November, stating that it was able to achieve a max RPM of 116,700 compared to a target of 117,000. This means they were able to achieve a mechanical RPM efficiency of 99.7%.
During the tests the engine achieved a corrected thrust of 23.67kgf, compared to a design thrust of 25kgf. They were able to achieve a corrected RPM of 98.3%.This shows that the engine has achieved a large amount of its target performance, however the company are still working on the project.
Small jet engine success
Micro jet engines are important for many new aerospace applications such as small UAVs, jet loitering munitions and other small airframes.
Creating these engines domestically would allow Indian manufacturers to limit their reliance on foreign propulsion systems. Vayuvya Defence have not stated any details about the Vayu 250 such as fuel consumption, endurance or the engines size, weight, life expectancy or what aircraft it will be integrated into. They have also not stated when they will be testing it on an aircraft or when it will go into production.
This means that it has been a successful test of the engine.
Qualifying the engine
However, the next stages of development for the Vayu 250 will be just as important. They must ensure that the engine can run at a sustained rate, manage its heat, be reliable, have low vibrations and be repeatable. Only then will it move closer to being integrated into an operational airframe.

articles.title: Nvidia places chip exports under boardroom supervision after Huang's exit
articles.text:
Nvidia's board has created a national security and export control committee amid intense scrutiny over co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang's departure and allegations that Singapore-based customer Megaspeed diverted GPUs to China.

The National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee, announced on Tuesday, will monitor Nvidia's national security policies, export compliance, and global trade risks. It will meet at least quarterly.

The committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and include directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members. Nvidia's existing National Security and Global Trade Compliance teams will report on day-to-day operations directly to this new committee, as well as to interim CEO Colette Kress.

The panel will oversee efforts to strengthen Nvidia's national security and trade compliance teams and retain independent legal, national security, and trade experts.

The announcement follows the resignation of Huang last week after he admitted to an affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive, and was allegedly involved in a second relationship with an Nvidia employee.

US authorities reportedly suspected Alice Huang of working for Chinese intelligence, an allegation that has not been proven. Megaspeed has separately faced scrutiny over suspected export control violations.

The US Department of Commerce and Department of Justice confirmed on Tuesday in a joint statement that they were investigating Megaspeed back in 2024. The agencies said they would pursue any criminal conduct uncovered by the investigation.

However, Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs stated that US authorities had provided only "limited assistance" when they were investigating the activities of Alice Huang and Megaspeed, as The Register reported.

The New York Times also reported that US investigations into Megaspeed were halted last year after an Nvidia executive contacted Commerce Department officials.

The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has issued new regulations tightening up restrictions on AI technology exports and cloud operators offering remote access to it.

The US also expanded its Pax Silica initiative, getting allied nations to sign an agreement that "guarding AI supply chains" is a shared responsibility.

Nvidia says it recognizes that advanced silicon and AI technologies present challenges for national security, and it has a responsibility to address them.

"We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation," said Harvey Jones, chair of Nvidia's board of directors. ®

articles.title: DRDO Lists Ram Accelerators and Plasma Guns in Research Roadmap
articles.text:
As part of its long term plans, the DRDO has identified several non-traditional options for gun development, including ram accelerators, magnetoplasma guns, light gas guns and regenerative liquid propellant weapons. This list can be found in their Technology Foresight document. However they have also identified several more recent improvements to be made, such as increased barrel life, recoil systems, improved ammunition handling and automatic weapon mounting.
This roadmap was released during a DRDO event called “Anusandhaan Chintan Shivir” on the 27th June 2023 in New Delhi. The roadmap identified 75 technology areas, which were split into 403 technology areas and 1295 active and future technology development goals. The Gun Technology area lists the ARDE as being responsible for developing the five technologies listed below.
Hyper Velocity RAM Gun (HVRG)
The most unusual of the list is the Hyper Velocity RAM Gun. This is to be developed by analysing supersonic flow inside the barrel, designing the ram accelerator barrel and projectile shape, and developing stoichiometric propellant loading. Ram accelerators utilise the motion of the projectile along a special combusting gas mix to increase the acceleration. This is very different to traditional gunfire where the propellant rapidly expands behind the projectile.
Magneto Plasma Gun
Another ambitious option is the development of the Magneto Plasma Gun. This will involve developing a bi-modular charge system with added plasma generating salts in the propellant, predicting the internal ballistics, and simulating contained plasma. Other developments will include magnetically containing the plasma using a pulsed power system and multi-layered solenoids.
Piston Compression Light Gas Gun (PCLG)
The list of developments for this gun system is shorter. This involves developing the breech mechanism and ammunition handling. While light gas guns are well known research tools for providing very high velocity projectiles, there is no information given on the performance of the system.
RArefaction waVE guN (RAVEN)
This weapon will involve integration onto a firing platform, synchronising the recoil, rarefaction wave and back blast, and designing the vent.
Regenerative Liquid Propellant Gun (RLPG)
This will involve developing the feeding mechanism and breech. Liquid hypergolic bi-propellants will be synthesised, and liquid propellant capsules will be designed. The weapon will also have regenerative injection and a high temperature resistant coating for the burning chamber. While this would provide more control over the propellant compared to traditional fixed ammunition, there is no indication that the weapon has been fully designed.
Improvements to increase longevity
There are several developments listed to improve traditional artillery. This includes developing composite barrels with metal inserts, thermal autofrettage, composite muzzle brake with metal liner, and erosion and wear resistant coatings.
Laser hardening and cryogenic coating will be applied to high calibre muzzle brakes. Nickel boron coatings will be used to improve the lifetime, reliability and cleanliness.
These are not trivial developments. Artillery operate under very high pressures and place large amounts of thermal and mechanical stress on the barrel and components. Increasing resistance to erosion, wear and thermal shock is therefore vital to ensure Indian guns can cope with intense firing profiles.
This is also relevant to the ATAGS. During trials at Pokhran in September 2020 there was a barrel explosion. Initial reports indicated concerns over the charge levels and pressures, however later reports indicated that the ammunition had failed due to faulty ammunition provided by the Ordnance Factory Board. This highlights the importance of looking at the gun and ammunition as a whole system.
Automatic Guns and new weapon stations
There are some interesting additions to the list. A medium calibre Cased Telescoped Weapon Station for vehicles, and a multi-barrel gatling gun for air defence.
The development of this gun will involve creating a 360 degree rotating slip ring mount, electrical actuators, rotating ammunition feed, misfire handling, electro optical and radar tracking, damage assessment after firing, and using AI to select weapons and automatically engage targets.
Threat engagement and ammunition selection for main battle tanks.
Research Focus
The Technology Foresight document is useful to see the range of technologies the DRDO wish to look into. From small improvements to increase barrel life to completely new ways of accelerating projectiles.
However the five advanced gun systems listed are just research goals. There is no indication of any prototypes, budget for development, service requirement or time frame.

articles.title: Website owners thumb their noses at EU privacy rules, researcher finds
articles.text:
Privacy? What privacy? The 100 most-visited English-language sites are flouting European data protection laws on a massive scale, according to a privacy researcher's investigation.

Forensic data analysis, published by Alexander Hanff, an attorney, computer scientist, and occasional contributor to The Register, with the support of SOMI (Stichting Onderzoek Marktinformatie), a Netherlands-based privacy group, details the dubious data flow.

From October 1 to 3, 2026, Hanff took a clean Google Chrome browser profile and measured what happens when the browser loads the 100 most visited English-language websites for five minutes, without any consent banner interaction.

At these 100 sites, visits were made to 265 pages – the home page, the privacy page, and the cookie notice when available – which resulted in 518,770 privacy events without any consent.

All 100 sites produced what the report characterizes as Tier 1 events – interception, exfiltration, or high-entropy fingerprinting (a total of 14,675). Tier 2 consists of storage on the device, capturing device characteristics, and script loads without consent (284,463 events recorded). Tier 3 includes protocol mechanisms and passive reads used for tracking (219,632 events).

The median website triggered 2,695 events, for a total of 28,695 events deemed high or critical. And 92.4 percent of the servers contacted during this process were on networks outside the European Economic Area (EEA). Most of these servers – 1,247 out of 1,400 – were in the US, and 1,034 belonged to third-parties.

The EU General Data Protection Regulation governs the transfer of personal data outside the EEA. The EU allows data transfers to the US for organizations participating in the EU–US Data Privacy Framework. Beyond that, according to Hanff and SOMI, a valid legal mechanism like a contract must be in place or the transfer may fail to meet GDPR or the ePrivacy Directive. In some cases, California Penal Code section 631 (interception) and section 502 (computer access) may also be relevant.

On these 100 websites, there were 89,437 fingerprinting events, 1,492 cookies set without consent, 7,456 scripts loaded from other origins, 18 websites implementing CNAME cloaking, and 37 websites delivering code to use the browser's built-in AI interfaces.

The privacy and cookie notices on these websites imposed a median reading time requirement of 28 minutes and none fully matched what their pages did. Among the sites' consent banners, 115 out of 165 used dark patterns, like steering visitors with emotional language about a "safer" or "better" experience, or "we care about your privacy."

The report, released in conjunction with a presentation at the Field Talk conference, also calculates the estimated environmental impact to load all this third-party content on websites without consent: 1,271,444 kWh per year, or enough to power 353 homes in Europe at 3.6 MWh per home annually.

SOMI is hosting a data finder to help people request access to the personal data companies have collected about them.

Hanff in an email told The Register that he would be shocked if these findings fail to get the attention of lawmakers and regulators in the EU, UK, and US, given plans to file privacy complaints with relevant authorities.

"Complaints will be filed against all of them and the EU supervisory authorities have a legal obligation to investigate them all – so we will have to wait and see," he said.

"One of the things we are discussing with SOMI is mass claims under the EU’s Representative Actions Directive but we are hoping that the industry and the regulators do the right thing so we don’t have to file lawsuits – again we will have to wait and see." ®

articles.title: India-Assisted Refurbished Soviet-Era Trainer Jet Flies From Kabul Airport, Videos Spark Debate

A Soviet-era trainer plane, believed to have been restored with help from Russia and India, flew out of Kabul Airport in its first flight for years, according to social media posts. The plane can be seen flying around the capital and airport in videos with the mountainous backdrop.

The Taliban has been trying to get older planes back up and running but there isn’t much verified information.
As there is no official statement from the Ministry of Defence, this has caused speculation. The videos have been taken as a sign that they may be trying to get them back up and running.
The fact that there has been some mention of India helping to restore the plane has caused some interest. While there is no official confirmation yet, if true it shows that there has been some quiet technical support from India.
What is clear is that this has brought attention to Afghanistan’s grounded fleet and the slow progress they have made to get them back up and running. It is unclear if this was just a one-off demonstration but until officials comment, these images will have to do most of the talking.

Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it
articles.text:
Researchers recently discovered unexpected behavior from Grok Bot, the AI agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Over five days, Grok bots installed on two separate employee laptops made 31 requests to access data stored in employee calendar, email, Slack, and GitHub accounts. The bots performed the actions even though the employees had never ordered them and continued doing them even after employees instructed them to stop. The bots also denied having taken the actions at all.

The behavior was reported Tuesday by NewCore, the maker of a managed gateway product that acts as an intermediary between AI agents and the tools and accounts they are assigned to work with. In some cases, the unapproved access attempts occurred while the laptop with Grok Bot installed had its lid shut, or late at night while the employee was sleeping. None of the unprompted actions were recorded in Grok logs. Without the gateway logs, the employees would have had no idea they occurred. And of course, without the gateway, the unapproved accesses would have succeeded—again without the end user's knowledge.

It’s “worse than a bug”

Once the employees learned that Grok Bot had tried to check in with accounts without prompting, one of them instructed the agent, four separate times, to stop taking any actions on its own. The agent's reply was: “I won’t set that up, and I’ll stop offering recurring check-ins.” Despite acknowledging the explicit instructions, the Grok Bot made more unapproved access attempts. When one of the employees asked the bot if it made any accesses, it checked twice and then outputted: “Overnight into Friday morning I was idle.”

Astra Microwave Products Limited has committed to deliver the initial two Uttam Active Antenna Array Unit (AAAU) radars to Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) by March 2027. The initial batch of 12 radars will be delivered by March 2028.
This revised delivery schedule was shared by the company’s management in its Q2 FY2026-27 results call. “HAL had targeted to get around 4 radars by March 2027. We have committed delivery of 2 radars by March 2027 but we are still trying to deliver 4 radars by then,” said Atim Kabra, Director – Strategy and Business Development, Astra Microwave.
“We have committed to deliver 12 radars by March 2028. We are working on our supply chain and manufacturing capacity to deliver them,” he added.
The Uttam radar order worth roughly ₹1,844 crore was awarded to the company by HAL and offers a large production opportunity. The radar will be fitted onto the Light Combat Aircraft Tejas Mk1A.
The revised delivery timeline is important given that the Tejas Mk1A project has suffered some delays due to the availability of the GE F404 engine. While delivering the radars will be an important step in delivering the aircraft, it is also important to note that this is an important component of the production process.
In its results call, Astra’s management also noted that they will be delivering 12 radars by March 2028. Delivery of additional radars depends on the production schedule.

India Joins US and Eight Countries to Secure Global AI Supply Chains
articles.text:
India, the US and eight other countries have signed a declaration to treat safeguarding artificial intelligence supply chains as a “shared endeavour” amid growing competition with China in emerging technology.The San Francisco Declaration was signed at a meeting of the founders of the US-led Pax Silica initiative convened by US Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg on Sunday.
The declaration was released by the Governments of the US, Australia, India, Israel, Japan, South Korea, Qatar, Singapore, the United Arab Emirates, and the United Kingdom.
The Pax Silica initiative was announced by the US in December last year to secure supply chains for silicon and other minerals essential to semiconductor production and, by extension, to artificial intelligence and other advanced technological industries.
The declaration on Sunday affirms that economic security is fundamental to national security, sets out the participants’ common understanding of the sensitive technologies and critical infrastructure that underpin Super Intelligence supply chains, and declares that safeguarding them is a shared endeavour, a State Department statement said.
The US government refers to Artificial Intelligence (AI) as Super Intelligence (SI) after President Donald Trump signed an executive order to rename it.
The Declaration on Secure Foundations of Enduring Prosperity also resolves to establish working groups to carry common purpose into common practice.It proposed to set up five groups covering pro-innovation policy frameworks, SI adoption in key sectors, supply chain cooperation across the SI stack, safe harbours and supply chain security hubs, and SI security and resilience.
“No nation can secure the foundations of the SI era alone, and the prosperity SI makes possible will only be as durable as the supply chains and infrastructure beneath it,” the statement said.
The declaration said that by agreeing on what must be protected and committing to protect it together, participants are laying the secure foundations on which partner nations can innovate, invest, and grow.
“Less than a year after its launch, Pax Silica is entering a new phase. With the San Francisco Declaration, the coalition cements its shared principles into a working partnership with a common baseline and a path to act on it, the statement said.

articles.title: GE May Ship 2–4 More F404 Engines for Tejas Mk1A in November
articles.text:
General Electric (GE) Aerospace will deliver between two to four additional F404-IN20 engines to Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) in November. This could mean cumulative deliveries of 16-18 engines by the end of the month.
The lastest indication shows that GE will be struggling to meet the four engines per month it was previously expected to deliver. At most they are likely to deliver around two to three engines.
In August 2026, GE delivered three engines. In September, four were delivered which means cumulative deliveries under the original 2021 contract reached 14.
The government did indicate that GE would deliver four engines per month in October, November, and December. This means 12 engines will be delivered in the last quarter of 2026. Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh said at the NDTV Defence Summit, “In October, November, December we’ll get 4 engines per month which will help HAL to speed up production.”
But the latest news shows that deliveries in November could be less than expected. If they deliver two, cumulative deliveries will be 16. If they deliver three engines, this will be 17. And if they deliver four it will be 18 by 30th November.
This makes December deliveries very important if HAL want to reach closer to the government’s original target of 22 engines by the end of 2026.
The F404-IN20 is the engine used on the single engine Tejas Mk1A. The original contract ordered 99 engines for the first 83 aircraft ordered by the IAF back in 2021.
GE’s late deliveries have been a huge issue for HAL to complete aircraft. They have many Mk1A airframes ready but they will still need engines, integration, ground testing and flight trials to be completed. The GE contract originally ordered 99 engines but a further order for 113 engines was placed to power the second batch of 97 Tejas Mk1A aircraft.
